A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TEMU-VTOFF, with matching research objectives and core architecture. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Dress Code and VITON-HD experiments, component ablations, and qualitative reconstructions in Tables 1–3 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds cross-dataset evaluations, downstream augmentation experiments, additional ablations, and a human preference study.

M1.justification: The main dual-DiT architecture, multimodal hybrid attention, and DINOv2 alignment procedure are retained. Appendix B/Table 7 adds an evaluated variant replacing CLIP with SigLIP 2 ViT-g/16 and introducing a 1536-to-2048-dimensional MLP projection, a limited architectural adaptation.

E1.justification: Both versions use Dress Code and VITON-HD, but v2 extends evaluation beyond within-dataset VTOFF. Section 4.3 adds transfer between the datasets, introducing domain-shift scenarios. Section 4.4 adds downstream VTON evaluation using synthetic person-garment pairs, substantially expanding task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MGT to Dress Code comparisons and adds published MGT, Voost, and One Model For All results to the VITON-HD comparison. Table 1 removes TryOffDiff's overall, lower-body, and dress comparisons while retaining upper-body results. Qualitative comparator membership also changes: Figure 4 replaces Any2AnyTryon with TryOffDiff.

E3.justification: v2 adds PSNR to the benchmark metrics and introduces cross-dataset testing, CatVTON training with versus without synthetic augmentation, and a randomized pairwise preference protocol involving 42 participants and 1,920 judgments. These substantially expand evaluation design. The original dataset splits and TEMU-VTOFF training budgets remain unchanged as reported.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained text, mask, and aligner ablations, v2 tests feature-extractor removal, alignment weights, alignment block depth, synchronous versus clean-feature timestep conditioning, and CLIP versus SigLIP 2. It also adds domain-shift robustness tests and per-image LPIPS/DISTS disagreement analysis in Figure 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The new user-study participant counts and randomized presentation describe evaluation design; its reported preference percentages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Shared numerical entries in Tables 1–3 are retained, but v2 adds PSNR, baseline scores, transfer and downstream results, sensitivity results, and preference rates of 75.77% against MGT and 77.74% against Any2AnyTryon. Expanded Table 2 changes the reported rankings: cited MGT and One Model For All results lead SSIM and LPIPS, respectively. TryOffDiff's non-upper-body Dress Code results are removed.

T1.justification: The core flow-matching, attention, and alignment equations retain their mathematical substance after matching reordered equations and notation. Algorithm 1 retains the same objective while renaming the generator loss from Ldiff to LDiT. New explanations of feature alignment and timestep choices are conceptual, without new proofs or formal derivations.

C1.justification: v2 removes the conclusion's claim that TEMU-VTOFF is the first approach to effectively extend VTOFF to multiple categories. Its abstract shifts emphasis from competitors' single-category restriction toward visual ambiguity and detail degradation. The central multi-category, dual-DiT, multimodal-attention, alignment, and state-of-the-art contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of the CLIP bottleneck, multiscale feature conditioning, alignment-depth tradeoffs, and clean versus noisy conditioning. It adds interpretations of downstream utility and human preference, plus a dedicated discussion of LPIPS/DISTS disagreement. Existing limitations concerning small text, buttons, textures, and lower-body imbalance are retained rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes garment-image training captions from person-image test captions, documents the aligner's training-only role, and specifies the SigLIP 2 projection. These disclosures do not establish that the original experiments used different inputs. Existing hardware and optimization details are relocated unchanged, while projector zero-initialization detail is omitted. Code/models are newly advertised as available, although the reproducibility statement still promises future release.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to cover MGT, Voost, One Model For All, and broader diffusion-conditioning approaches such as ControlNet, T2I-Adapter, and IP-Adapter. Additional discussion connects the design to CleanDIFT and ConceptAttention. Acknowledging existing multi-category and bidirectional systems revises the novelty positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial methodology passages are rewritten, with feature extraction, modulation, and training explanations reorganized. Implementation details move to the appendix, caption extraction is integrated into its details section, and broader impact becomes an ethics statement. The experimental narrative and appendix organization are substantially revised.

P2.justification: v2 expands Tables 1–3 with metric columns and comparison or ablation rows, adds Tables 4–8, revises the architecture diagram, and replaces several qualitative panels. It adds an inference-caption illustration and a per-image metric figure, alongside conference-format layout changes. The original appendix component-ablation grid and both failure-case panels are retained under new numbering.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily supported its design through within-dataset comparisons and limited component ablations, while practical augmentation benefits remained untested. v2 adds direct transfer and downstream tests, isolates important architectural choices, supplies human-preference evidence, and clarifies test-time caption inputs. These address substantial validation and reproducibility gaps despite unchanged original scores. Uncertainty estimates remain absent and release-status wording is inconsistent, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence.
